label: Blue Note
rationale: Joe Henderson's third Blue Note album pairs him with Kenny Dorham plus two members of the Coltrane quartet — McCoy Tyner and Elvin Jones — and Richard Davis on bass, three weeks after the same rhythm nucleus cut Andrew Hill's Point of Departure. The title track pushes hard bop to its breaking point; 'Punjab' and 'Serenity' became standards. Strong consensus: AllMusic 4.5 stars, Penguin Guide 3.5 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4 stars.

personnel_record.notes: Single session, April 10, 1964, Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs (S1 infobox, S3). S2 (AllMusic) records the same date but lists location as 'New York, NY' — a broad metro reference; Van Gelder Studio, Englewood Cliffs is the better-sourced value and both are recorded here. Producer Alfred Lion per S1 infobox and S3. Engineer not named in sources; Blue Note session at Van Gelder Studio in 1964 implies Rudy Van Gelder — recorded with epistemic inf per the Van Gelder inference rule; epistemic_production inf. CD reissue adds an alternate take of 'In 'N Out' — excluded as reissue-only. Year recorded as 1964 (recording year; released early 1965 per S1). AllMusic legacy page r140573 serves correctly; newer mw-IDs rotted. Side A/B split follows the original LP sequence (tracks 1-3 / 4-5).

ballot.case_for: This is an exceptionally consequential post-bop session: Joe Henderson and Kenny Dorham are backed by McCoy Tyner, Elvin Jones, and Richard Davis, connecting Blue Note hard bop directly to the contemporaneous Coltrane and Andrew Hill currents (S1, S3). Its title track stretches hard-bop energy and form without crossing into excluded free jazz, while the dossier identifies "Punjab" and "Serenity" as tunes that entered musicians' repertoire. Critical signals are strongly favorable—AllMusic rates it 4.5 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 4 stars, and Penguin 3.5—and its personnel and sustained discovery value make it a powerful document of 1960s post-bop.
ballot.case_against: The evidence supports an excellent record more clearly than an indisputable canon-lock statement. Penguin's 3.5-star rating, without a Core Collection designation or crown, and the absence in the dossier of independent canon-list appearances leave its cross-tradition consensus materially below the strongest consensus-core cases. Henderson's Page One and Inner Urge have stronger claims to be his defining Blue Note-era statements, so In 'n Out must justify itself as more than a superbly staffed transitional session; the dossier's sourcing is also weighted toward an overview source and a label feature rather than multiple independent critical histories.
ballot.disagreement: The references agree on scope and strong priority but split on tier: one finds the extraordinary Tyner-Jones-Davis session and repertoire impact sufficient for consensus_core, while the other regards the modest Penguin distinction, thin independent canon-list evidence, and competition from Page One and Inner Urge as a real basis for contested status.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John treat In 'n Out as a strong contested candidate, favoring it for its session gravity while weighing whether its distinct load-bearing role exceeds Henderson's more definitive albums.
